name: GET operation retries on 503
description: Verifies that GET operations automatically retry on 503 Service Unavailable with exponential backoff. The success body uses the legacy single-key envelope, which every runner unwraps to a bare array before the wire; project_count 0 pins that unwrap parity (an enveloped body leaks through as 1 pseudo-item).

name: GET operation retries on 429 with Retry-After
description: Verifies that 429 responses respect the Retry-After header

name: POST operation does NOT retry (not idempotent)
description: Verifies that POST operations do NOT retry since they are not idempotent

name: Non-retryable error not retried
description: Verifies that 404 errors are not retried

name: Retry-After HTTP-date in the past falls through to backoff
description:
SPEC §6 step 2 honours an HTTP-date only when `date - now()` is positive. A past date yields a non-positive value, so the algorithm must fall through to step 3 — the backoff formula — and the pin is `delayBetweenRequests`, not the retry itself.

This replaces a case that asserted only `requestCount: 2` and `noError` against the same past date. Those two assertions are satisfied identically by a parser that never looks at dates at all: it fails the integer parse, backs off, and retries. That is why Kotlin's missing HTTP-date branch (#564) survived a green conformance suite for the SDK's entire life — measured against un-fixed Kotlin and un-fixed TypeScript, the old case passed in ~1.0s, which is precisely the backoff it was meant to be distinguishing the date from. The delay pin gives the case something to fail on: a parser that returns the negative difference, or clamps it to 0 and honours that, retries with no wait — the shape TypeScript's `retry.ts` had before #564.

What this case still cannot see is the POSITIVE half of step 2, which needs a date a few seconds ahead of the run's own clock. A fixture is a static JSON literal and the harness has no clock: a date far enough ahead to stay future-dated would make every compliant SDK sleep for years (Retry-After is exempt from SPEC §7's backoff ceiling, so nothing clamps it), and a date near enough to assert a small delay against is past-dated within seconds of being written. The positive branch is therefore pinned by per-SDK unit tests — Kotlin's `parseRetryAfterParsesFutureHttpDate`, TypeScript's `errors.test.ts` — and #780 tracks giving the harness a clock so this fixture can cover it.

name: Retry-After of 0 is rejected and falls through to backoff
description:
`0` is a well-formed `delay-seconds`, and SPEC §6 step 1 deliberately declines to honour it: the integer branch returns a value only when it is > 0. `0` is not an HTTP-date either, so step 3 applies and the retry waits the ordinary backoff rather than firing immediately.

Red against TypeScript before #564: `retry.ts` read the header with `parseInt` and no `> 0` guard, so `Retry-After: 0` became a 0 ms sleep and the backoff collapsed entirely. `requestCount` cannot see that — a collapsed backoff still retries, and still succeeds — so `delayBetweenRequests` is the whole assertion here. The second TypeScript copy of the same algorithm, on the multipart upload path in `services/base.ts`, guarded with `>= 0` and so admitted zero explicitly; conformance reaches only the JSON client path, so that copy is pinned by a TypeScript unit test instead.

name: Negative Retry-After is rejected and falls through to backoff
description:
`-5` fails step 1's `> 0` guard and is not an HTTP-date, so SPEC §6 lands on step 3. RFC 9110 spells `delay-seconds` as `1*DIGIT`, which makes a negative value malformed input rather than an instruction — and the contract is that malformed input costs the caller a normal backoff, never a SHORTER wait than a well-formed value would have bought.

Red against TypeScript before #564: `parseInt("-5")` is a number and passed the `!isNaN` gate, so `retry.ts` computed a delay of -5000 ms and slept for a negative interval, retrying at once. That is the same collapsed backoff as the zero case reached by a different route, which is why both are pinned rather than one standing in for the other: the `>= 0` guard on the upload path rejected this value while admitting zero, so a single case would have found only half the defect.

name: Partly numeric Retry-After is rejected and falls through to backoff
description:
RFC 9110 spells `delay-seconds` as `1*DIGIT`, so SPEC §6 step 1 must validate the WHOLE value rather than read a number off the front of it. `120junk` is not 120 seconds; it is malformed, and malformed input costs the ordinary backoff.

Five SDKs got this free from their integer parsers — `strconv.Atoi`, `int()`, `Integer(exception: false)`, `Int()` and `toIntOrNull()` all refuse a trailing-junk value — and TypeScript alone did not, because `parseInt` stops at the first non-digit and returns what it has. That made a malformed header worth a 120-second delay in one SDK and ~1s in the other five, inside the very algorithm this file exists to keep uniform. The case is added alongside the zero and negative ones because it is the same shape and the other five pass it unchanged, which is exactly what makes it worth pinning: it converts five accidental agreements into one stated contract.

name: POST with 429 is not retried
description: Verifies that POST operations receiving 429 are NOT retried since POST is not idempotent (2B.4)

name: 403 Forbidden is not retried
description: Verifies that 403 Forbidden errors are not retried since they lack @retryable (2B.5)

name: GET 500 is not retried
description: 500 is absent from every operation's declared retryOn [429, 503]; the declared set gates status retries in all six SDKs, so a 500 must surface after exactly one attempt. Pins the #485 Ruby fix: its error taxonomy calls 500 retryable, but the taxonomy must not widen the declared set for governed traffic.

name: max_retries 0 sends exactly one request on a governed operation
description:
`max_retries = 0` is a legal spelling of "no retries — exactly one attempt", not a request to send nothing (SPEC §2 validation step 4). Until #718 the spec said `⊥` here and hand-written Go agreed by panicking at construction, while the other four numeric SDKs already accepted and floored the value — a contradiction with SPEC §14's own attempt-budget table, which had blessed "a zero cap" as yielding exactly one attempt all along.

`GetProject` is governed: it carries a `retry.max` of 3 in behavior-model.json, and 503 is in its declared `retry_on` set, so every retrying SDK would otherwise make three attempts here. In Go this case is red twice over against un-fixed code — first because client construction panicked, and then, once it did not, because the typed operation ran on the generated client's DefaultRetryConfig and made three requests: `initGeneratedClient` never passed the caller's cap at all.

A single 503 is queued deliberately: an SDK that retried would send a second request, fall off the end of the queue and get the mock's end-of-queue 500, so `requestCount: 1` cannot pass vacuously — it fails on the count either way.

**Strength is not uniform across the six runners, and this fixture does not pretend otherwise.** Go, Python, Ruby and Swift consult the budget BEFORE the first request (pre-check loops), so a zero cap is a real regression guard there. Kotlin and TypeScript consult it after, so a budget of 0 and of 1 are observably identical in those two — the same asymmetry #713 hit. TypeScript additionally has no numeric cap at all: the override maps to `enableRetry: false`, which is its spelling of the same contract (SPEC §2 validation step 4), as it does in Swift.

name: max_retries 0 sends exactly one request on ungoverned download traffic
description:
The companion to the governed case, on the one conformance-reachable path with NO operation entry in behavior-model.json. Every modelled operation in behavior-model.json carries a retry block, so "ungoverned" cannot mean an operation that lacks one — it means traffic with no operation ID at all, and `DownloadURL` is the reachable example (SPEC §14 hop-1 retry). With no per-operation ceiling to clamp it, the client cap is the entire budget, which is what makes this the case where a missing floor is unmasked rather than hidden behind a `min(cap, op_max)`.

503 is in the hop-1 retry set, so a retrying SDK sends a second request here. In hand-written Go the download loop is a separate pre-check loop from the GET one and needed its own floor: against un-fixed code a zero cap skipped it entirely and returned a usage error having sent nothing.

A single 503 is queued deliberately: an SDK that retried would send a second request, fall off the end of the queue and get the mock's end-of-queue 500, so `requestCount: 1` cannot pass vacuously — it fails on the count either way.

**Strength is not uniform across the six runners, and this fixture does not pretend otherwise.** Go, Python, Ruby and Swift consult the budget BEFORE the first request (pre-check loops), so a zero cap is a real regression guard there. Kotlin and TypeScript consult it after, so a budget of 0 and of 1 are observably identical in those two — the same asymmetry #713 hit. TypeScript additionally has no numeric cap at all: the override maps to `enableRetry: false`, which is its spelling of the same contract (SPEC §2 validation step 4), as it does in Swift.
